doc.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Worst situations and playing with musicians of every culture
summary: He cannot recall a worst situation, believes in making the best of any gig, and lists the world musicians he has worked with.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: How about the worst musical situation?
Oh man, the worst? I honestly can’t tell you because I think I put it out of my mind.

Yeah. Well I think everything is a learning situation. And I believe that I’ve learned that the idea is to try to take a bad situation and make it as good as possible, as long as you’re there. And if you can’t do that then you should leave. So that’s pretty much how I operate. And if I feel I have to leave and I don’t want to do that then I try to keep that out of my realm. Because I believe in accentuating the positive and eliminating the negative. So that’s generally — so I honestly don’t remember what maybe was the worst situation.

Well it’s a good thing for students to think about, you know, like what you’ve done from playing with Blues bands on the south side, to doing Afro-Cuban music and absorbing all that, to get your own voice.

Well the world is much smaller than it used to be. And that’s a good thing. I’ve had opportunity to play with musicians from every culture, from Japanese, shakuhachi flute players, to Indian tabla players, I’ve worked with Haitian musicians, I’ve worked with African musicians, and when I say Africa, Africa as a continent not a country, so I’ve worked with musicians from Senegal, from Ivory Coast and they’re different, from Mali, and Chinese music. It’s really been, for me that’s been a great thing. Cuban musicians, Puerto Rican musicians, musicians from — Panamanian.
